artboards.title: Proposed — a band filtered, naming a day, and no cash figure
Proposed — settled, not started, and failed to read

annotations.text:
THE JOB OF THIS SCREEN

You settled four things, and everything here follows from them.

1. THE CONSTRAINT LEADS. You said the screen is where you decide who gets paid next — so the first figure on it is what is actually in the drawer, not what you owe. "You owe 12,400,000" is half a sentence; the question is always what can be paid today.

2. THE QUEUE IS RANKED BY WHAT TO PAY FIRST, not by age. A day you named and let pass, then days you have given, then whoever has waited longest. That order is stated in the panel head and again in the rail, because a list that reorders itself without saying why is a list nobody trusts.

3. NAMING A DAY HAPPENS ON THE BILL. The whole "When you said you would pay" panel — three sub-lists, its own paragraph, and a prompt() box — is gone. A day is a fact about ONE bill, so it is named on that bill's line inside the open supplier, where the amount and the age are already on screen to name it against.

4. THE ACCENT IS "PAY THIS SUPPLIER", once, inside the one open row.

AND THE TITLE IS NOW "CREDITORS". The rail said "Who you owe", the heading said "Creditors list", the breadcrumb said "Who you owe" — three names for one screen, the same fault Debtors had. "Who you owe" stays as a search keyword, so the words already in somebody's head still find the door.

Everything is drawn from index.html's own values: the 23-colour palette, the 11/12/13/14 ramp, Inter + Archivo Black + IBM Plex Mono, and the .ow-* console components already shipping on Today, Debtors, Chase debts, Follow-ups and Consignment. No new colour, no new weight, no new type size, no fourteenth button family.

WHAT IS WRONG WITH IT AS IT STANDS →

1. THREE NAMES FOR ONE SCREEN. Rail: "Who you owe". Heading: "Creditors list". Breadcrumb: "Who you owe".

2. A 240-CHARACTER PARAGRAPH IN THE PAGE HEAD, unmeasured, sitting open above the money. The console header is a name, one line, a hairline; the long version goes behind the "i". Debtors, Chase debts, Follow-ups and Consignment all do this already — this screen and the old page-head are what is left.

3. THE HEADLINE FIGURE IS IN THE WRONG FACE. .age-pos-total b sets 12,400,000 in Archivo Black at 34px. Archivo Black is loaded for PAGE NAMES ONLY; money is IBM Plex Mono, tabular. 34px is not on the ramp either.

4. THE BAR AND THE BAND CARDS SAY THE SAME THING TWICE — a 16px stacked bar, then five bordered cards repeating the same five figures, and both are the filter. About 120px of height spent saying one thing in two voices.

5. TWO COLOURED VERDICT BLOCKS STACKED. Crimson "over 90 days", then amber "in hand today". Both are facts the strip can carry as tiles; as prose blocks they push the list down and argue with each other for the eye. The cash figure especially is buried at the BOTTOM of the panel — the one number you came to the screen with.

6. THE SECOND CONSOLE. "When you said you would pay" is a whole screen inside this screen: its own paragraph, three headed sub-lists, and up to five buttons per line. On a book of 23 bills it is roughly 900px before the list you came for.

7. IT IS DRIVEN BY prompt() AND confirm(). Naming a day opens a browser dialog asking for YYYY-MM-DD typed by hand. On a phone in a yard that is a dialog nobody fills in — and it is the act that decides whether 940,000 appears on the cash line in What's coming.

8. EXPORT AND PRINT SIT IN THE PANEL HEAD, one heading above the search box that decides what they will contain.

9. THE CONTROLS DO NOT LOOK LIKE CONTROLS. Search is a .field with a floating label; "Hide no balance" is a bare checkbox nudged with padding-bottom:9px, and reads as a double negative.

10. THE SAME FACT TWICE ON EVERY ROW — a coloured age pill AND a 3px coloured stripe on the first cell. Every row has an age, so every row is coloured, and a device that marks everything marks nothing.

11. SEVEN COLUMNS, AND THE ONE THAT DECIDES THE ORDER IS NOT AMONG THEM. You can sort by owed, waiting, bills or last paid — but nothing on the row says whether you gave this supplier a day and let it pass, which is the single fact that decides who gets paid first.

12. THE BAND FILTER IS ECHOED IN A NOTE BELOW THE TABLE, after the rows it removed, in a panel of its own.

13. OFF-SYSTEM VALUES THROUGHOUT — sizes 10.5, 11.5, 12.5, 13.5, 34; radii 10 and 999 where the system is 4/6/8; a drop shadow where depth in this app is hairlines.

THE PROPOSAL — what changed, and why

THE STRIP LEADS WITH WHAT IS IN THE DRAWER. Four questions and not one more: what you hold today and what share of the book it covers; what you owe (stated as the whole book, whatever the list is filtered to); what is past a day you named — crimson, because a broken word is what a supplier actually stops delivering over, and it beats "over 90 days" as the bad-news tile since it is about your conduct rather than the calendar; and what falls due inside a week, amber, already on the cash line in What's coming. "In hand" is ink, not a state colour: money you hold is a fact, and colouring it would make an ordinary Tuesday look like an alarm.

THE WATERLINE. The one device this screen has that Debtors does not. Rows are ranked by what to pay first, and a dashed level across the list says how far today's cash reaches: "paying down this list in full, the 4 above come to 4,720,000 of the 4,850,000 in hand. The 5 below wait on money coming in." It states its own assumption in the same breath, so it reads as a measurement and not as the app having decided who gets paid. Nothing below it is dimmed — a figure the shop owes is not less true for being further down the page.

WHEN THERE IS NO CASH FIGURE THERE IS NO LINE. See page 2: the tile goes amber and says the cash book has not been opened today, and where the line would have been the screen says why it cannot be drawn, with the door to fix it. It does not draw a line from a zero it invented.

A ROW CARRIES THE REASON IT IS WHERE IT IS. The column Debtors does not have: "12 days past your word — you said 22 Aug" in crimson, "You said 6 Sep — in 3 days" in amber, "No day named — on 2 of the 3" in plain grey. Age moves to the basis line under the figure, where it is the only place age lives on the row. So the pill and the stripe are both gone and the colour in a row means something.

THE OPEN ROW IS THE BILLS, AND WHERE A DAY IS NAMED. Bill, dated, waiting, the day you named, still open. The day cell carries the date with how it stands — 5 days past, in 3 days — and a pencil; a bill with no day carries "Name a day". That replaces prompt() entirely, and page 2 shows it open: a date field, "Write it down", and one amber line saying exactly what writing it down will do to the cash line. No modal, no dialog, no typing YYYY-MM-DD from memory.

THE THREE SUB-LISTS ARE ACCOUNTED FOR, NOT DROPPED. Every bill was in exactly one of three states — no day, a day ahead, a day gone by — and the old panel's job was to make sure none fell out of sight. That job is now done in three places at once: the two tiles at the top of the strip, the reason column on every row, and the rail's "of the 23 bills open, 7 carry a day". Nothing is invisible; it just is not a second screen any more.

THE TOOLBAR IS A TOOLBAR — search with a magnifier in it, a real toggle reading "Hide settled" rather than "Hide no balance", then Print and Export pushed right, all in one 46px band directly above the rows they act on. Print says "Print these 3" when a band is on.

THE RAIL CARRIES THE REASONING, MEASURED. How the order is worked out (so the ranking is never a black box), four derived figures, what a payment does — oldest bill first, posted to the cash book as a stock purchase, part payments keep their original age — and what naming a day does, with the count of how many bills carry one and the door to What's coming.

HEIGHT: the two panels above the list went from roughly 1,100px to 300px. Four suppliers and the waterline are on the first screen where previously the list had not started.

A BAND FILTERED, A DAY BEING NAMED, AND NO CASH FIGURE →

All three at once, because they are the states that interact.

THE FILTER IS VISIBLE IN THREE PLACES. The segment and its legend entry are ringed, an amber chip sits in the toolbar with its own ✕, and the note under the list says what is hidden — "6 suppliers owed 10,220,000 between them are not listed" — and, crucially, that each figure above is that band's SHARE rather than the whole balance. A smaller figure beside a familiar name otherwise reads as the balance having changed.

THE ROWS SAY IT TOO. Under a filter a row's basis line gains a second line: "waiting 88 days / of 2,940,000 owed in all". And the open row's caption says "over 90 days only", with the footer noting that 2 of the supplier's 3 bills are outside the band — because Pay settles their oldest bill first whichever band it is in, and that is a real trap if the screen does not say so.

THE STRIP DOES NOT MOVE. Still 12,400,000 across 9 suppliers. The existing code's own comment says why: a position that shrinks because somebody left a filter on is a position nobody can trust.

NO CASH FIGURE, NO WATERLINE. The tile reads "Not known" in amber — not 0 — and where the line would be, the screen says it cannot be measured and offers the door. This is the app's own law: derived, never invented, and a failure must name itself. cbDayPosition() creates a day record as a side effect, so this screen must not call it just to render — which is exactly why the figure can be genuinely absent.

NAMING A DAY, OPEN. A date field, "Write it down", Cancel, and one amber line: what it will do to the cash line in What's coming, what it will NOT do (it does not pay anything and it tells nobody), and that it is your own note of what you intend. The old prompt() said some of this in a dialog nobody reads.

THE THREE STATES A SCREEN IS ONLY DESIGNED ONCE YOU HAVE DRAWN →

NO STRIP OF ZEROS. Four tiles reading 0 fills a settled screen with figures that mean nothing and makes a straight book look like a broken screen. One sentence is the whole state.

SETTLED AND NOT STARTED ARE WORDED DIFFERENTLY, which the current code already gets right on this screen and is worth keeping. A shop that has never bought on credit has not "settled every bill" — it has not begun. The second wording also names where bills come from, since nothing here is recorded by hand: a bill is raised when a quote is marked invoiced.

THE THIRD STATE IS MISSING TODAY. If the supplier ledger fails to read, this screen shows "You owe nothing to anybody" — a failed load and a settled book are indistinguishable, and only one of them means you owe nothing. The app's own law says a failure must name itself. So it says what failed, when the last good read was, that these are not your balances, and it turns Pay off rather than letting a payment land against a bill nobody can see.

The settled state still carries two real figures, because "everything bought on credit this month has been paid" is the one reading of an empty creditors book worth anything.

All three are stacked here to compare the wording. In the app only one is ever on screen.

THE PHONE — its own design, not the table reflowed

820px is a switch, so this is drawn from scratch at 390: 44px navy bar, 26px page name, 15px body, 14–16px row padding, 44px hit targets.

THE PHONE JOB IS DIFFERENT FROM THE DESK JOB. At the desk you are working down a list deciding a day's payments. On a phone you have just paid somebody, or a supplier has called to ask when. So: the 2×2 strip leads with what is in hand, search sits high, and the cards carry the REASON line prominently — "12 days past your word" — because that is the sentence you need when the supplier is on the line.

THE WATERLINE SURVIVES, TURNED. A centred rule with text either side has no room at 390px, so it becomes a full-bleed band between the cards with a small caps label above the sentence. Same fact, same wording, one column.

THE BAR SURVIVES, THE LEGEND TURNS. Five bands across 358px is unreadable as five columns, so the legend becomes band-and-figure pairs.

THE CARDS CARRY NO BUTTON. A Pay button on every card is nine oxide buttons on a screen allowed one, so the accent lives once, in the docked navy bar in the thumb zone — the pattern Follow-ups and Debtors already ship. It names who to pay first, so the default action is right without reading the list, and it follows the search result.

NO FAKE CHROME: no painted status bar, no fake keyboard.

ONE THING TO DECIDE: whether the phone should let you PAY at all, or only read and name days. A payment posts to the cash book, and a mis-tap in a yard is a wrong ledger entry. I have drawn it enabled because paying a supplier is exactly what happens away from the desk — say the word and it becomes read-only with the dock naming a day instead.

WHAT I HAVE NOT DECIDED FOR YOU

1. THE RANKING RULE ITSELF. Broken word → day given → oldest. That is my reading of "who a supplier stops delivering over", and it is stated on screen so it can be argued with. If you would rather it were simply biggest-first, or oldest-first like Debtors, it is one comparator.

2. "PAID OFF" IS GONE FROM THE ROW. Debtors keeps a progress bar because a customer part-paying is a signal about them. On the buy side the part-payer is YOU, and how far through your own bill you are does not decide who to pay next — the reason column took its place. The figures still exist; say the word and the bar comes back.

3. THE WATERLINE'S ASSUMPTION. It assumes paying down the list in full, in order. The honest alternative is a running "left after this" column on every row, which is more precise and much busier. I chose the line. 

4. "DUE IN THE NEXT 7 DAYS" — seven is my number, not yours. It could be a rule you set, the way Chase debts has its grace period.

5. THE OLD NAME. "Who you owe" and "creditors list" stay as search keywords so the word already in your head still finds the screen.

6. WHAT I HAVE NOT TOUCHED: the Pay modal itself, the CSV, and the printed sheet — beyond the printed sheet needing to say which filter it was printed under, as Debtors now does.
